# 243 — PR explainer

*Read top to bottom; the diff is described in reading order at the end.*

*Tier: HIGH, as the spec's own risk tier called it — a generated SEO surface at estate scale (87
chain pages, freshly measured, the same file family as the sacred sitemap-adjacent generators),
touching every chain page's direct-answer/FAQ content.*

---

## The goal

Item 242 built `headlinePoolFor(pools)`: given a page's displayed pools, pick the single pool that
(a) has the highest rate AND (b) passes 229's `isRepresentativeRate` check — falling back to the
plain highest-rate pool only if nothing passes. 242 wired that into the 2,102 static
`/tokens/<symbol>` pages and explicitly ticketed the identical fix for the chain estate as this
item, naming the exact lines. This item does exactly that: reuse the same function, at the same
two call sites (HTML render + its markdown twin), on `generate-chain-pages.js` instead of
`generate-token-pages.js`.

Before this item, a chain page's headline rate was `Math.max(...rec.pools.map(poolTotalApy))` —
the single most extreme number on the page — attributed to `rec.pools[0]`, the TVL-largest pool.
Those are very often *different pools*. So a chain page could say "the highest yield on Ethereum
is 694.11% on Protocol A" when Protocol A's own pool pays 20% and the 694% belongs to some other,
unnamed pool on the same page.

## The intuition

Same one sentence as 242: **a headline number and the name printed next to it must always come
from the same pool.**

```js
const bestApy = Math.max(...rec.pools.map(poolTotalApy));   // the pool with the highest rate
const top = rec.pools[0];                                    // the pool with the most TVL
buildAnswerAndFaq(rec.chain, rec, bestApy, top, language);   // rate from ONE pool, name from ANOTHER
```

Nothing here is new math — it is the identical gap 242 closed on token pages, on a different file
that happens to repeat the exact same two lines. There is no local `isRepresentativeRate`
re-implementation to write and no new predicate to design: `generate-chain-pages.js` already
`require()`s `generate-token-pages.js` and destructures a long list of shared helpers from it
(`poolTotalApy`, `buildAnswerAndFaq`, etc.) — `headlinePoolFor` and `isRepresentativeRate` just
needed to be added to that same list.

## Why the blindspot check mattered here

The spec explicitly asked: does `renderChainHubPage` (the /chains index page) independently
compute a headline rate anywhere? If it did, that would be a THIRD call site of the identical
defect, silently out of scope unless flagged. Reading it end to end: it renders a title, a
description that only cites `ranked.length` (a page count, not a rate), and a flat list of
`<a href=".../chains/<slug>">` links built from chain name + slug only. It never calls
`poolTotalApy` or `buildAnswerAndFaq`, and `grep`ing the whole file for `Math.max`/`bestApy`
confirms exactly two matches — both inside the two functions the spec already named. **Verdict:
no third call site, honestly checked, not assumed.**

## What changed and why

**1. No new implementation — reuse only.** `headlinePoolFor` and `isRepresentativeRate` added to
the existing `const { ... } = tp;` destructure at the top of `generate-chain-pages.js`. No new
`require`, no local definition, no second implementation to drift out of sync with 242's.

**2. One pool, one claim — HTML (`renderChainPage`).**
```js
const headlinePool = headlinePoolFor(rec.pools);
const bestApy = poolTotalApy(headlinePool);
buildAnswerAndFaq(rec.chain, rec, bestApy, headlinePool, language);  // same pool, both args
```
`top = rec.pools[0]` is untouched — it still feeds `tcpChainIntro`'s "here's this chain's biggest
pool" sentence, with its own honest APY. That line was never wrong; it just isn't the headline.

**3. The identical substitution — the markdown twin (`renderChainPageMarkdown`).** Same three
lines, same call. One deviation from 242's exact code shape: the markdown twin has no intro line
that uses `top`, so once `buildAnswerAndFaq`'s 4th argument became `headlinePool`, `top` had zero
remaining readers in that function and was dropped rather than left declared-and-unused —
matching 242's own token-side markdown twin, which never declares `top` either.

## What did NOT change

The visible pool table (still every displayed pool, TVL-sorted, unchanged order — proven by a
test), which chains get a page at all (`rankTopChains`'s gates untouched), the chain sitemap, the
per-chain yield-headline KPI line (`yieldHeadlineFor`, which was never `bestApy`-based to begin
with), `renderChainHubPage`, every trust rail (`APY_SANITY_LIMIT`, `MIN_POOL_TVL`, anomaly
exclusion), and the entire token-page estate (untouched, and `test_token_pages.js`'s 109/109 still
passes — proof of no cross-surface regression).

## The diff, in reading order

1. **`generate-chain-pages.js`, the `const { ... } = tp;` destructure**: `headlinePoolFor,
   isRepresentativeRate` added.
2. **`generate-chain-pages.js`, `renderChainPage`**: `bestApy`/`buildAnswerAndFaq`'s 4th arg
   switch from `Math.max(...)`/`top` to `headlinePoolFor(rec.pools)`'s result.
3. **`generate-chain-pages.js`, `renderChainPageMarkdown`**: the identical change (`top` dropped,
   per the deviation above), so the two twins can never state different numbers for the same page.
4. **`test_chain_pages.js`**: a new `243 —` block — a fixture population (four chain records, each
   grouping several pools under the SAME `chain` value, run through the real `rankTopChains`),
   checked for the headline-APY invariant, the attribution invariant (project matches the headline
   pool, in both the answer block and FAQ A1, EN and KO), markdown-twin parity, two positive
   controls lifted from 242's own worked numbers, and an unchanged-surface proof (table order,
   `rankTopChains` idempotence, sitemap output unaffected).

## Deviations worth knowing about (full detail in `243-notes.md`)

- The markdown twin's `top = rec.pools[0]` was dropped rather than kept-but-unused, since the
  chain markdown page has no intro line that reads it — matching 242's own precedent on the token
  side rather than leaving an inconsistency between the two twins' code shape.
- The attribution-invariant test checks only the headline pool's PROJECT, not its chain (242's
  token-page version checks both). On a chain-page record every pool shares the SAME `chain` value
  by construction (that is what `rankTopChains` groups by), so asserting chain-name inclusion
  would be true regardless of which pool were selected — it would not discriminate the actual
  defect (a page naming the wrong protocol).
- A direct sitemap-unaffected check was added to the unchanged-surface-proof block, since this
  item's own acceptance criteria name the chain sitemap explicitly (242's token-side section
  relied on the `rankTopTokens`-idempotence proof to imply the sitemap-equivalent claim; here it
  is checked directly).
- The re-measured live numbers land at a much smaller page count (87 chain pages vs 242's 2,102
  token pages) but a substantially HIGHER mismatched-attribution rate (60.9% vs 20.0%) — chain
  pages aggregate more pools per page on average, which raises the odds that the TVL-largest pool
  and the highest-rate pool are different pools. Full table in `243-notes.md`.

## Quiz

1. Why did this item not need to write a new `headlinePoolFor` or `isRepresentativeRate`
   implementation anywhere?
2. The spec asked for an explicit blindspot check on `renderChainHubPage`. What did that check
   look for, and what was the actual finding?
3. `top = rec.pools[0]` survives untouched in `renderChainPage` but is REMOVED entirely from
   `renderChainPageMarkdown`. Why the difference between the two twins?
4. The attribution-invariant test for chain pages checks the headline pool's project but
   deliberately does NOT check its chain, unlike 242's equivalent token-page test. Why is that
   omission correct rather than a gap?
5. The live re-measurement shows chain pages have a LOWER rate of pools failing
   `isRepresentativeRate` (12.0%) than token pages did in 242 (25.0%), yet a much HIGHER rate of
   mismatched old-headline attribution (60.9% vs 20.0%). What structural difference between the
   two page types explains that combination?
